title_en: GM106: What Happens When the Debt Finally Matters ft. Marvin Barth
title_zh: GM106：当债务终于变得要紧时会发生什么 —— 对话 Thematic Markets 的 Marvin Barth
subtitle_zh: Marvin Barth 与 Cem Karsan 激辩美国债务、通胀预期与民粹主义，探讨美联储的出路。
description: GM106: What Happens When the Debt Finally Matters ft. Marvin Barth

turns.en: The critical driver of inflation is expectations, nothing else. Like, yes, you can create inflation. Otherwise yes, there will be short term shocks to inflation, but if inflation's expectations are stable, inflation will come back to where it was. The problem is the Fed allowed inflation expectations to get out of control and that's why we're not going to get inflation expectations back down until the Fed does something about them.
turns.zh: 通胀最关键的驱动因素就是预期，别的都不是。当然，你可以人为制造通胀，短期内也会有各种冲击，但只要通胀预期是稳定的，通胀最终会回到原来的水平。问题在于美联储放任通胀预期失控了，所以在美联储出手之前，我们别指望通胀预期能降下来。

turns.en: Welcome to top traders Unplugged in markets, success doesn't come from predicting what happens next. It comes from being prepared for what you can't predict. In each episode, we go deep with some of the world's most thoughtful minds in investing, economics and beyond to understand how they think, how they prepare and how they decide, and the experiences that shaped how they see the world. No noise, no shortcuts, just real conversations to help you think better and invest with Conf.
turns.zh: 欢迎收听 Top Traders Unplugged。在市场里，成功并不来自于预测接下来会发生什么，而是来自于为你无法预测的东西做好准备。每一期节目，我们都会与投资、经济以及其他领域里一些最有思想深度的人深入交流，理解他们如何思考、如何准备、如何决策，以及那些塑造了他们世界观的经历。没有噪音，没有捷径，只有真实的对话，帮你更好地思考、更有把握地投资。

turns.en: Marvin, welcome to the podcast and thank you so much for joining Cem and I for what I know will be a fascinating conversation with you. You come highly recommended by our recent guest and friend Dave Dredge. So, we are super excited to have you here. Marvin, how are you doing?
turns.zh: Marvin，欢迎来到我们的节目，非常感谢你加入 Cem 和我，我相信这会是一场非常精彩的对话。你是我们最近的一位嘉宾、也是我们的朋友 Dave Dredge 大力推荐来的，所以我们特别高兴你能来。Marvin，你最近怎么样？

turns.en: I am well. Thank you for having me on. Niels. Cem, pleasure to finally come on the show. I'm a big fan. You guys have a great podcast. Thank you so much. Thank you so much. Has it been a quiet summer for you or has kind of the global macro environment sort of kept you from switching off completely?
turns.zh: 我很好，谢谢你们邀请我，Niels。Cem，很高兴终于能上你们的节目，我可是你们的忠实粉丝，你们这档播客做得太棒了，非常感谢。谢谢，谢谢。这个夏天过得清静吗，还是说全球宏观的大环境让你根本没法彻底放松下来？

turns.en: Well, you know, I uncharacteristically decided to take a month off. So for last month I've been off. Supposedly off. Right.
turns.zh: 嗯，你知道，我这次一反常态地决定休一个月假，所以过去这一个月我一直在休假，算是休假吧。对吧。

turns.en: And you know, one of the things I like to emphasize about my research is that it has a very, very long shelf life. So, you know, I routinely have people asking me for reports I wrote a decade or more ago because they're still relevant. And so what I did is I set up, ahead of time a whole spate of emails every two days to all my clients and subscribers that highlight things going on and say, hey, here's what I've written on that topic in the past and that's been great. The more important thing for
turns.zh: 而且，我想强调我研究的一个特点，就是它的“保质期”特别特别长。所以经常有人来找我十年前甚至更早写的报告，因为它们到今天依然有参考价值。于是我提前设置好了一大批邮件，每隔两天自动发给我的客户和订阅者，点评当下正在发生的事，然后说“嘿，关于这个话题我以前是这么写的”，效果非常好。更重要的是，

turns.en: me is I have finally gotten a chance to just decompress and start to think deep thoughts again after what has been, I think, for everyone, a frenetic 18 months.
turns.zh: 对我而言，我终于有机会彻底放松下来，重新开始思考一些有深度的问题——毕竟过去这18个月，我想对每个人来说都是忙得脚不沾地的。

turns.en: Right. You know, President Trump, whatever you think of him one way or the other, is a human volatility machine. In fact, I've described him as a antidote to Minsky moments. Right. It's impossible for too much risk to build up in the system with that guy there because there is something new every single day. Right. And even for somebody who, for the most part, I would say, actually called everything he was doing quite correctly ahead of time, that didn't help. It didn't matter. Like, it's just so frenetic. So for me,
turns.zh: 对。你知道，Trump 总统，不管你怎么看他，他本人就是一台人形波动率制造机。事实上，我把他形容成明斯基时刻（Minsky moments）的解药。对。只要有他在，系统里就不可能积累起过多的风险，因为每天都会有新花样冒出来。对。而且即便对某个基本上、可以说对他每一步动作都提前判断得相当准确的人来说，那也没用，也没帮上忙。就是太折腾了。所以对我来说，

turns.en: contrary to most people, it actually has been a relatively quiet summer, just simply because I got to disengage for the last month, even though the rest of the world kept going.
turns.zh: 和大多数人相反，这个夏天其实过得相当清静，就因为在过去这一个月里我得以抽身出来，尽管世界其他地方还在照常运转。

turns.en: Yeah, no, indeed. Cem, what about you? Any decompression in Chicago this summer, or.
turns.zh: 是啊，确实。Cem，你呢？这个夏天在芝加哥有没有好好放松一下，还是？

turns.en: I would say I'm in this brief little eddy in the river this summer. It's been a busy, busy summer. I. My kids are back and my son's about to go off to boarding school. So this is a beautiful week or two of just reconnecting at 15.
turns.zh: 我会说，这个夏天我处在河里一个短暂的小漩涡里。这是个忙得不可开交的夏天。我的孩子们回来了，我儿子马上要去寄宿学校了。所以这是难得的一两周美好时光，好好重新联络一下感情，他都15岁了。

turns.en: Yeah. Good stuff. Fantastic. Yeah, yeah. Now, since it's your first time on the podcast, Marvin, I did want, you know, for the audience to get a little bit of sense of your background. It's pretty impressive. But instead of just doing the usual list of all the kind of prestigious jobs you've had, I thought maybe, maybe I could ask you to pick. And I know it's a bit unfair when you don't know that I'm going to say this, but maybe you could pick two or three kind of pivotal
turns.zh: 好，真好，太棒了。好。那么，Marvin，既然这是你第一次上我们的节目，我确实想让观众对你的背景有点了解，你的履历相当亮眼。但与其照例把你干过的那些显赫职位一一列出来，我想或许可以请你挑一挑——我知道在你不知道我要这么问的情况下这有点不公平——但也许你可以挑两三个关键的

turns.en: points in your career where you experienced something profound, maybe that kind of shaped how you think today and which ultimately led you to where you are today and having set up thematic markets
turns.zh: 职业节点，你在那些时刻经历了某些深刻的东西，或许塑造了你今天的思维方式，并最终把你带到现在这个位置，创立了你现在经营的 Thematic Markets。

turns.en: that you run today. Okay, so let me start with something early, which was I largely worked my way through university, and I worked actually a bunch of odd jobs, but I'll highlight two. I worked in a Heinz tomato ketchup factory, and I worked as a commercial salmon fisherman in Alaska. And the reason why I highlight those, I used to put those on leave, particularly the salmon fishing on my resume.
turns.zh: 好，那我先从早期说起。我基本上是自己打工读完了大学，干过一堆杂活儿，但我要重点说两个。我在 Heinz 番茄酱工厂干过，还在阿拉斯加当过商业三文鱼渔民。我之所以要强调这两段，是因为我以前会把它们、尤其是打鱼那段写在简历上。

turns.en: Just because any job interview that's immediate gives people a conversation point. You are a fisherman in Alaska. Yeah, but I mention it here because, you know, I think that's given me a very different perspective than most people in markets. Right. Most people in markets come from. This is not universally true, but come from very similar backgrounds, went to the same schools, did the same things throughout. And it limits their ability to see a lot of the social and political trends that you would see if you were working
turns.zh: 就因为任何一场求职面试都能立刻给人一个话题切入点：“你是在阿拉斯加打鱼的？”是的。但我在这里提它，是因为我觉得这给了我一个跟市场上大多数人很不一样的视角。对。市场上大多数人来自——这一点并非放之四海而皆准，但——非常相似的背景，上同样的学校，一路做着同样的事情。这就限制了他们去看到很多社会和政治趋势的能力，而这些趋势，如果你是和

turns.en: with different sets of people who are from socioeconomic groups that most people on Wall street or in London never really come across. So I would say that's been very pivotal to My career, it's just given me different perspective than most people. The next thing I would say was going to the Federal Reserve. So when I was at the Federal Reserve, I started in emerging markets.
turns.zh: 来自不同社会经济群体的人一起工作，你就会看到——那些群体是华尔街或伦敦的大多数人从来不会真正接触到的。所以我觉得这一点对我的职业生涯非常关键，它就是给了我一个跟大多数人不一样的视角。我要说的下一段经历是进美联储（Federal Reserve）。我在美联储的时候，是从新兴市场做起的。

turns.en: I was actually dropped into the hot seat. I was thrown in to be the Southeast Asia desk officer right in the middle of the East Asian crisis back in 98. But as soon as that died down, I moved to what's called the Financial Markets Group, which briefed the board every week on global market developments, foreign exchange developments, and was working very closely with the senior staff.
turns.zh: 我实际上是被直接扔进了火线。1998年东亚危机正酣的时候，我被推上去当了东南亚事务的 desk officer。等那场危机平息下来，我就转到了所谓的市场组（Financial Markets Group），每周向理事会汇报全球市场动态、外汇动态，跟高层同事密切合作。

turns.en: And the wonderful thing about that was we used to have this morning call to go over the morning operation. Both of you are old enough to remember the Fed used to actually intervene in the market every day to get the Fed funds rate where it wanted, rather than this ample reserves policy they have now. And so as a result, you had to have a call to approve what the program was for, how much reserves they were going to add or subtract from the system. And. And you would have, you know, Karen Johnson, Mike
turns.zh: 那份工作最棒的一点是，我们每天早上都有一个电话会，过一遍当天的公开市场操作。你们俩年纪都够大，应该记得美联储以前是真的每天都会入市干预，把联邦基金利率调到它想要的位置，而不是像现在这样搞什么“充足准备金”（ample reserves）政策。所以结果就是，你必须开一个电话会来批准当天的操作方案，要往系统里加多少准备金、或者抽走多少。而且，你会有，你知道，Karen Johnson、Mike

turns.en: Prel, Don Kohn sitting there with you. These people had each been, you know, the Barons, the three research directors for 20 years.
turns.zh: Prell、Don Kohn 跟你坐在一起。这些人每一个都当过，你知道，那几位“男爵”——三位研究部主任，干了20年。

turns.en: They had more experience than anyone you've seen in your career. They've been through everything. And you would every morning have a call and one of them would say, oh, yeah, this reminds me of the dollar crisis in 1978. And, you know, you just absorbed.
turns.zh: 他们的经验比你职业生涯里见过的任何人都丰富，他们什么都经历过。你每天早上开会，其中某一位就会说：“哦，对，这让我想起1978年的美元危机。”然后你就在潜移默化中吸收。

turns.en: It was way better than any economics lesson I could ever have because I had people who were in the room making decisions, who,
turns.zh: 这比我能上的任何一堂经济学课都要好得多，因为坐在我面前的，都是当年亲自在决策现场做决定的人，他们

turns.en: three of them, teaching me firsthand about economic history of the basically post Bretton woods period. And then the third point was, when I left the Fed, I started to. I had effectively sort of maxed out on what I felt was my learning curve and I wanted to try new things. And so I left and I went. One of my former mentors from the Fed had gone to Citi, and I followed him there.
turns.zh: 三个人，手把手地教我基本是布雷顿森林体系（Bretton Woods）之后的经济史。然后第三段经历是，当我离开美联储的时候，我已经基本上把我能学到的东西学到了头，我感觉自己的学习曲线到顶了，就想尝试些新东西。于是我离开了。我在美联储的一位老导师去了 Citi，我就跟着他过去了。

turns.en: And for the first time, I was responsible for putting together sort of a general equilibrium view, if you sort of use economist speak, that is, how do you put together the whole global view, how all these assets fit together? Because the Fed, you know, like most places, you're relatively siloed, but I was in currency research and I had to actually figure out how it all came together. And I had all this training, but that was a real shock to learn how everything works together. So I would say it's those three. If
turns.zh: 那是我第一次负责搭建一个所谓的一般均衡视角（general equilibrium view）——如果用经济学行话来说——也就是说，你怎么把整个全球图景拼起来，所有这些资产是怎么相互契合的。因为在美联储，跟大多数地方一样，你是相对割裂的、各管一摊，而我当时在做外汇研究，却不得不真正搞清楚这一切是怎么拼到一起的。我受过所有这些训练，但要真正弄明白万物如何联动，那真是一次不小的冲击。所以我会说，就是这三段。如果

turns.en: you were going to pick three events, those would be the three that really had the largest effect on shaping how I think about the world.
turns.zh: 非要挑三件事的话，那三件就是对我如何看待这个世界影响最大的三段经历。

turns.en: Okay, that's pretty cool. All right. Okay, so let me try and kind of set the scene for the first question or topic, and then I know that my good friend Jim will come in and we'll go in different directions and that's going to be super, super interesting. So, you know, for the better part of three decades, central banks has kind of rested on a fairly powerful idea that if policymakers understand the economy well enough, set interest rates appropriately and manage expectations carefully, they can smooth out the
turns.zh: 好，那挺酷的。好，那么我先来给第一个问题、或者说第一个话题铺垫一下背景，然后我知道我的好朋友 Cem 待会儿会插进来，我们会往不同方向聊，那会非常有意思。你知道，在差不多三十年里，央行的运作基本上都建立在一个相当有力的理念之上：只要决策者足够了解经济、把利率设置得当、并小心地管理好预期，他们就能熨平

turns.en: business cycle and keep inflation reasonably stable. That broad framework became kind of the intellectual consensus insight.
turns.zh: 经济周期，并把通胀保持在相当稳定的水平。这套大框架后来成了主流的知识共识。

turns.en: Central banks, you can disagree if you, if you want later on. But after years of, let's call it extraordinary monetary policies and the inflation shock, we had many forecasting errors. And now we have Kevin Walsh openly basically questioning how the Fed thinks about the economy. It feels as though we may be confronting something much bigger than just the next move in interest rates.
turns.zh: 在央行圈里，这一点你后面可以不同意。但经过多年的、我们就叫它非常规货币政策吧，再加上那轮通胀冲击，我们出现了很多预测失误。现在 Kevin Warsh 又公开地质疑美联储理解经济的方式。感觉我们面对的东西，可能远远不只是利率的下一次调整。

turns.en: So perhaps the question is whether the entire framework gave policymakers more confidence in their ability to manage the economy than just was ever justified. So, Marvin, we could of course start with, you know, one way would be to say what exactly the new Keynesian economics promised us and was the mistake the model itself, or that central bankers eventually started believing the model too much. Or we could get right into the current debate among that's happening among three people who used to work together,
turns.zh: 所以，也许真正的问题是，整套框架是不是给了决策者超出其实际应有程度的信心，让他们以为自己有能力管理经济。那么，Marvin，我们当然可以先从——一种切入方式是说说新凯恩斯主义经济学（New Keynesian economics）到底向我们承诺了什么，以及问题究竟出在模型本身，还是出在央行官员最终太过相信这个模型。或者我们也可以直接进入当下正在三个人之间上演的辩论，这三个人以前是共事过的，

turns.en: namely Stanley Druckenmiller, Scott Bessant and Kevin Walsh. Because I think that is also kind of topical at the moment. So you can kind of choose your path here.
turns.zh: 也就是 Stanley Druckenmiller、Scott Bessent 和 Kevin Warsh。因为我觉得这个话题当下也挺应景。所以你可以自己选一条路来聊。

turns.en: Yeah, so look, the only disagreement or quibble I might have with the way you frame the question was that it's been three decades that, that economists in central bank have thought that they can manage things. Frankly, it goes back many more decades than that. And of course they got in the last time they really thought they understood what was going on was the 1960s. And of course that's when they sowed the seeds for the great inflation that they had. Because nothing brings you down like arrogance. Right.
turns.zh: 嗯，你看，我对你这个提问方式唯一有点不同意、或者说想挑剔一下的地方是：你说经济学家和央行以为自己能驾驭一切已经有三十年了。坦白讲，这往回追溯远不止三十年。而且，上一次他们真的以为自己搞懂了状况，是在1960年代。当然，那正是他们为大通胀（great inflation）埋下祸根的时候。因为没有什么比傲慢更能让人栽跟头了。对。

turns.en: This is like a rule in life. And I think that's the underlying problem. And the reason why I bring that up is because the exact same thing happened. You went through a period of, you know, critical thinking in economics. What did we get wrong? How did we do this?
turns.zh: 这几乎是人生的一条定律，我觉得这就是问题的根源。我之所以提这个，是因为一模一样的事情又发生了。你经历了一段经济学界的批判性反思期：我们到底哪里搞错了？我们是怎么搞成这样的？

turns.en: And it sort of diverged. You had big debates within economics through the 70s and 80s into the early 90s. In the meantime, you know, Alan Greenspan came in and yeah, there were a lot of really sort of fortuitous tailwinds for him. But the fact was, Alan Greenspan was actually a really interesting guy. I mean, I'm still a huge Alan Greenspan fan as a central banker. He wasn't a particularly nice guy personally, by the way, but he was a fantastic central banker for all the people want to complain about him. And part of
turns.zh: 然后它就分化了。整个70年代、80年代一直到90年代初，经济学界内部有很多大辩论。与此同时，Alan Greenspan 上任了，是的，他赶上了很多非常有利的顺风。但事实是，Alan Greenspan 其实是个非常有意思的人。我是说，作为一个央行行长，我至今仍是他的超级粉丝。顺便说一句，他这个人私下并不算特别友善，但不管有多少人想批评他，他都是一个极其出色的央行行长。而其中一部分

turns.en: that was, is that he did accept that we didn't know everything. He didn't succumb to that arrogance problem. But he managed the economy so well. And in the background, other economists were coming in and bringing in this new Keynesian framework beginning in the 1990s. And people started to think, especially in academic academia, that, wow, we really nailed this. We really know what we're doing now. And the new Keynesian synthesis offered an amazing number of really powerful insights into economics. But. But
turns.zh: 原因在于，他确实承认我们并非无所不知，他没有陷入那种傲慢的问题。而且他把经济管理得非常好。与此同时，在背景里，其他经济学家开始引入这套新凯恩斯主义框架，始于1990年代。人们开始觉得，尤其是在学术界，哇，我们真的把这套东西吃透了，我们现在真的知道自己在干什么了。新凯恩斯主义综合（New Keynesian synthesis）为经济学提供了数量惊人的、非常有力的洞见。但是，

turns.en: it has a lot of flaws. And most importantly, it is a model. It is not reality. And it's always really important to keep that in mind. And I think a lot of people lost sight of that and tried to apply it much too directly to the economy. And we've seen the results of that. We've seen error after error after error. And it results from the same sort of hubris that we saw before that effectively, there was this belief that somehow economists had all the knobs and dials and they could just turn everything as
turns.zh: 它有很多缺陷。而最重要的是，它是一个模型，不是现实。始终牢记这一点非常非常重要。我觉得很多人忽略了这一点，试图把它过于直接地套用到经济上，我们也看到了后果——一个接一个的错误。而这些错误，都源于我们之前见过的那种同样的自负：人们相信经济学家手里握着所有的旋钮和表盘，可以随意拧动，把经济调到自己想要的

turns.en: they needed to and get the economy to exactly where they were. And when it didn't work out, they said they never lost faith in themselves. Right. They would always say, we just need to try this new thing from our model or this path. Right. And so I've used this analogy for regulation as well in my writing, but it applies very, very well to this situation. I don't know if you, either of you have ever come across this story about. There once was this little old lady who swallowed a fly, and then she swallowed
